column4: The section explicitly develops فَارِغًا here: Moses' mother's heart is an emptied vessel, while God's binding of it keeps that emptied heart from disclosing her secret.
رَبَّنَا أَفْرِغْ عَلَيْنَا صَبْرًا makes patience something poured over Saul's outnumbered company; the following request to steady their feet shows what that filling enables.
The threatened magicians ask رَبَّنَا أَفْرِغْ عَلَيْنَا صَبْرًا: divine patience is poured into people facing death, exactly the section's bucket metaphor.
أُفْرِغْ عَلَيْهِ قِطْرًا is the section's literal emptying sense: molten copper is poured over the heated iron until the structure is consolidated.
The section cites وَحُصِّلَ مَا فِي الصُّدُورِ as the contents of breast-vessels being brought out and exposed.
وَأَلْقَتْ مَا فِيهَا وَتَخَلَّتْ gives the fullest nonlexical parallel: the earth casts out its contents and becomes empty like a discharged vessel.
The earth is first stretched out in وَإِذَا الْأَرْضُ مُدَّتْ; this enlarged container is the one that empties itself in 84:4.
After emptying in 84:4, the earth hearkens to its Lord; that sequence parallels the section's emptied vessel followed by orientation to the Lord.
The human being labors toward the Lord and will meet Him, closely joining the section's فَانصَبْ with وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ even without its vessel words.
أَفَمَن شَرَحَ اللَّهُ صَدْرَهُ لِلْإِسْلَامِ repeats the expanded breast and states what fills that new capacity: Islam and light from one's Lord.
God's يَشْرَحْ صَدْرَهُ لِلْإِسْلَامِ is set against a breast made ضَيِّقًا حَرَجًا, defining the section's enlarged inner volume by its exact opposite.
Moses' prayer رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي asks the Lord to enlarge the inner vessel so it can bear the work and speech that follow.
إِنَّا إِلَى اللَّهِ رَاغِبُونَ closely restates the section's final direction, while God's promised bounty supplies the source dictionary's sense of a great gift one desires.
The prophets call upon God رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا; desire becomes a prayerful orientation to God rather than an appetite left to itself.
This ayah unusually gathers both images: thirst, نَصَبٌ, and hunger are endured, while believers are forbidden أَن يَرْغَبُوا بِأَنفُسِهِمْ عَن نَّفْسِهِ, reversing self-directed desire.
Rain fills valleys بِقَدَرِهَا, each according to its capacity, and the flood bears off foam while useful matter remains; the image tests vessel-size by what it can receive and retain.
The water drawer lowers دَلْوَهُ into the well and draws Joseph out, staging the bucket and wellhead that underlie the section's concrete sense of emptying.
At Midian's water Moses finds a whole community watering and two women held back; the well is a place of ordered access and turns, as in the section's water-round.
Moses waters for the women, then turns to his Lord as one in need of any good sent down; watering is followed immediately by Godward desire for provision.
God makes a flowing spring of molten copper, عَيْنَ الْقِطْرِ, turning the same material poured in 18:96 into a water-source image beside the huge vessels of 34:13.
جِفَانٍ كَالْجَوَابِ are great basins like reservoirs, the Quran's closest concrete counterpart to the section's wide hollow basin.
A struck stone releases twelve springs, each people knows its drinking place, and all are told to eat and drink from God's provision: stonework, water turns, and filling meet.
Twelve springs issue from the struck stone and every tribe knows its drinking place, directly staging apportioned water at stone sources.
At the river Saul limits drinking to a single handful; measured appetite at water immediately precedes the prayer that God pour patience in 2:250.
The she-camel has one drinking share and the people another on an appointed day, giving the section's wellside image a literal water-turn.
الْمَاءَ قِسْمَةٌ بَيْنَهُمْ makes water an apportioned turn, with each drink attended in sequence.
Water is sent down بِقَدَرٍ, lodged in the earth, and can be taken away; the ayah joins measured filling, storage, and possible emptying.
Job names his affliction نُصْبٍ وَعَذَابٍ; the root's toil sense is immediately answered in 38:42 by a water source for washing and drinking.
After the نُصْب of 38:41, Job strikes the ground and receives a cool bath and drink, bringing exertion to a restorative water-place.
Water descends from heaven to cleanse, remove inner defilement, bind hearts, and steady feet; it unites poured water with the heart-binding of 28:10 and the steadied feet of 2:250.
وَرَبَطْنَا عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمْ repeats God's act of binding hearts, showing the same divine stabilization that keeps the empty heart in 28:10 from spilling its secret.
وَأَفْئِدَتُهُمْ هَوَاءٌ depicts hearts as hollow or vacant, a direct nonlexical counterpart to the heart emptied of patience in 28:10.
Golden platters and cups circulate while the Garden contains مَا تَشْتَهِيهِ الْأَنفُسُ; vessels and appetite meet in a gift that truly answers desire.
Silver vessels and crystal cups are passed around the blessed, placing the container itself inside the scene of abundant provision.
The crystal vessels are قَدَّرُوهَا تَقْدِيرًا, measured to their proper amount; volume and provision are fitted to one another rather than appetite being limitless.
وَسَقَاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَرَابًا طَهُورًا explicitly joins the Lord with the giving of drink, making concrete the section's movement toward the source of gathered water.
وَكَأْسًا دِهَاقًا presents a cup filled to abundance, the positive completion of an emptied container.
أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا الْمَاءَ صَبًّا uses the very verb with which the source dictionary explains emptying a bucket, but makes God the giver who pours water for food.
The command فَلْيَعْبُدُوا رَبَّ هَٰذَا الْبَيْتِ directs response to the Lord, and 106:4 identifies Him as the one who fills hunger and secures fear.
Feeding مِن جُوعٍ makes the Lord's provision the answer to the empty, hungry belly developed in the section.
إِنَّا أَعْطَيْنَاكَ الْكَوْثَرَ is an overflowing grant of abundance, closely matching the source dictionary's رغِيبة, a great gift desired.
The abundant gift in 108:1 is followed by فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ, the same movement from received bounty to action directed exclusively to one's Lord.
لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا states that obligation is fitted to inner capacity; it explains why enlargement of the breast matters when a burden is borne.
Spending is scaled to what one has been given, and God promises ease after constraint; provision, capacity, and what may be poured out are held in one measure.
God sends water down and gives it as drink while humans are not its keepers, وَمَا أَنتُمْ لَهُ بِخَازِنِينَ; the filled store ultimately belongs to the giver.
Stones split and water comes out, while others fall in awe of God; the section's upright well-stones are returned here to their life-giving source and Godward stance.
The gates of heaven open بِمَاءٍ مُّنْهَمِرٍ, a torrent poured down before waters gather in 54:12.
Springs burst from the earth and the two waters meet عَلَىٰ أَمْرٍ قَدْ قُدِرَ, combining gathered abundance with exact measure.
The earth is ordered to swallow its water and the sky to withhold, until وَغِيضَ الْمَاءُ; the flood-container is emptied under divine command.
مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ اللَّهِ بَاقٍ contrasts what is exhausted with what remains with God, giving the emptied vessel a reason to turn toward its inexhaustible source.
Even if the sea were ink for the Lord's words, the sea would be exhausted first; the largest visible reservoir still empties before divine abundance does.
A sea replenished by seven more seas cannot exhaust God's words, expanding the section's wide reservoir image beyond every finite capacity.
Abraham identifies the Lord as the one who feeds and gives drink, joining the filling of hunger and thirst to proper Godward dependence.
The graves are overturned and their contents raised before the breasts' contents are exposed in 100:10, enlarging the emptying scene beyond the chest alone.
وَأَخْرَجَتِ الْأَرْضُ أَثْقَالَهَا makes the earth discharge its burdens like a container emptied of what weighed inside it.

The source defines farāgh first as the opposite of occupation; سَنَفْرُغُ لَكُمْ uses that root idiomatically for God's concentrated reckoning, a consequential sense distinct from pouring out a vessel.
The barrier can neither be scaled nor pierced after copper is poured in 18:96; this result shows that emptying the molten contents has made the structure firm.
Moses' mother is told to cast him into the river and trust the promise of his return; this supplies the water-separation that leaves her heart empty in 28:10.
Moses is restored to his mother so her eye may be cooled and she need not grieve, completing the divine refilling and reassurance of the emptied heart in 28:10.
Rain is threaded into springs in the earth, raises vegetation, and leaves it dry debris; a stored water-source fills living forms and then visibly runs out.
The question أَفَرَأَيْتُمُ الْمَاءَ الَّذِي تَشْرَبُونَ turns attention from the drinker's appetite to the water itself.
The next question asks whether people sent water from the cloud or God did, identifying the true provider at the far end of the vessel.
God could make the drinking water bitter; the desired filling of the vessel is therefore a gift rather than an entitlement.
Cups, ewers, and a cup from a flowing spring combine portable vessels with an unconfined water source.
A cup from a flowing spring is passed among the blessed, pairing a bounded drinking vessel with abundant source-water.
A running spring supplies the water-side of the Garden scene whose cups are set out in 88:14.
وَأَكْوَابٌ مَّوْضُوعَةٌ places ready vessels beside the running spring of 88:12, a peaceful counterpart to the section's well and basin.
نَصِيبَكَ here means one's allotted share, while the ayah directs God's gift toward seeking the Hereafter; the source dictionary's homonymous نَصِيب, a stone basin, makes portion and receptacle meet.
One who desires the Hereafter's harvest receives increase, while one who desires the world's gets some of it but no نَصِيب in the Hereafter; appetite is defined by its chosen destination and share.
Moses says the journey has brought نَصَبًا just after passing the meeting of the two seas; the root's toil sense occurs inside a water-journey rather than the source dictionary's stone-basin sense.
وَإِلَى الْجِبَالِ كَيْفَ نُصِبَتْ uses the root for massive stones set upright, clarifying the physical act behind the source dictionary's basin built from erected stones.
The nursing household's food, clothing, and duty are limited by لَا تُكَلَّفُ نَفْسٌ إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا, applying vessel-like capacity to bodily provision and care.
Justice in measure and weight is followed by لَا نُكَلِّفُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا; capacity is a limit to obligation as surely as volume limits a vessel.
The people of the Garden are introduced with لَا نُكَلِّفُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا, linking the final abundance with a life whose demands fit human capacity.
No soul is charged beyond its capacity, and a truthful record stands with God; the inner vessel has a divinely known limit.
God tests what is in the breasts and purifies what is in the hearts, treating the inner self as a container whose contents can be examined and refined.
Whatever believers spend, God replaces; what is poured out in faithful use is answered by the Provider rather than guarded as a permanently full private vessel.
Whatever people are given is temporary enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting for those who rely on their Lord; desire is redirected from finite contents to their source.
وَمَا صَبْرُكَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ states directly that the addressee's patience comes only through God, supplying the agency behind the section's image of patience poured down.
When the Prophet's breast is constricted in 15:97, he is told to glorify his Lord and prostrate, answering inner constriction with directed worship.
The command to worship the Lord until certainty comes continues the response to the constricted breast, much as the section ends by directing effort and desire toward the Lord.
مَن شَرَحَ بِالْكُفْرِ صَدْرًا uses the same opening of the breast for willing unbelief, showing that enlarged capacity is defined also by what one chooses to admit.
فَلَا يَكُن فِي صَدْرِكَ حَرَجٌ forbids constriction in the Prophet's breast as he receives the Book and warns, the negative boundary of the expanded breast.
وَضَائِقٌ بِهِ صَدْرُكَ names the Prophet's breast tightening under hostile demands, reversing the spaciousness granted for his charge.
The Prophet's breast narrows because of what opponents say; 15:98-99 then direct that constrained interior toward praise, prostration, and worship.
Moses fears rejection and says وَيَضِيقُ صَدْرِي, a mission-bearing chest constricted where his later prayer asks that it be expanded.
The earth becomes narrow for the three بِمَا رَحُبَتْ and their own selves constrict; objective spaciousness cannot fill an inwardly closed person.
If the community's water sinks away, no one else can bring flowing water; the full basin is bounded by the giver's power to leave it empty.
A garden's water can sink so deep that its owner cannot retrieve it, reversing the accessible well and abundant pool of the section.
بِئْرٍ مُّعَطَّلَةٍ is an abandoned well amid destroyed settlements, a water-place whose social use and turns have ceased.
One who calls on others is like a person stretching hands toward water that will never reach the mouth; failed drinking becomes a precise reversal of desire directed to the true Lord.
مَن يَرْغَبُ عَن مِّلَّةِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ uses رغب with عَنْ for aversion, reversing the section's رغب with إِلَىٰ and exposing the importance of desire's direction.
أَرَاغِبٌ أَنتَ عَنْ آلِهَتِي asks whether Abraham turns away from the idols; the same root with عَنْ marks withdrawal rather than desire toward the Lord.
People rush from graves كَأَنَّهُمْ إِلَىٰ نُصُبٍ يُوفِضُونَ, as if racing toward a raised marker; the destination reverses the command to direct desire toward the Lord.
الْأَنصَابُ are erected cult stones declared defilement; they oppose the source dictionary's erected stones that support a life-giving well.
Animals sacrificed عَلَى النُّصُبِ make erected stone a site of forbidden devotion, the opposite use from stones forming a water basin.
The Garden's inhabitants are touched by no نَصَبٌ and never expelled; toil is a present command whose final Godward destination has no fatigue.
In the lasting abode, لَا يَمَسُّنَا فِيهَا نَصَبٌ; the laboring sense of the root ends where divine bounty does not run out.
كُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا وَلَا تُسْرِفُوا places an explicit boundary around eating and drinking, correcting the source dictionary's wide-bellied gluttony.
Good provision may be eaten, but appetite must not become excess; the gift that fills can turn destructive when its measure is ignored.
Those who merely enjoy themselves and eat كَمَا تَأْكُلُ الْأَنْعَامُ embody the ungoverned, wide-bellied appetite named in the source dictionary.
A secure town once received abundant provision from every place, then tasted enveloping hunger after ingratitude; fullness becomes emptiness when the gift's source is denied.
The response to the hungry town's example is to eat lawful good provision and thank God, setting gratitude as the boundary of appetite.
The people of Hell fill their bellies from the tree of Zaqqūm, a horrifying realization of the section's large belly rather than a desirable great gift.
After their bellies are filled, they receive a mixture of boiling water, joining unchecked appetite to a punishing drink.
Zaqqūm is like molten substance inside the bellies, bringing the section's poured metal and wide interior together as punishment.
The molten food boils in bellies like scalding water, turning both vessel and liquid against the eater.
ثُمَّ صُبُّوا فَوْقَ رَأْسِهِ مِنْ عَذَابِ الْحَمِيمِ reverses patience poured over believers: boiling punishment is poured over the condemned.
فَمَالِئُونَ مِنْهَا الْبُطُونَ makes belly-filling explicit, but the contents are Zaqqūm rather than the bountiful gift desire seeks.
The filled bellies are followed by drinking boiling water, joining appetite and water in a ruined feast.
They drink like desperately thirsty camels, an image of appetite that cannot find its measure even while being filled.
يُصَبُّ مِن فَوْقِ رُءُوسِهِمُ الْحَمِيمُ uses literal pouring from above, but the emptied liquid vessel delivers torment rather than patience.
The poured boiling water melts what is inside their bellies, turning the body's interior from a capacity for provision into a site of dissolution.
فَصَبَّ عَلَيْهِمْ رَبُّكَ سَوْطَ عَذَابٍ retains both pouring and your Lord but makes the poured content punishment, the sharp inverse of poured patience and desired bounty.
Those consuming orphan wealth unjustly eat fire into their bellies, exposing the moral content hidden inside voracious intake.
Those who trade away revelation for a small price consume nothing but fire into their bellies, a spiritual boundary on the image of the great eater.
The Prophet is told not to stretch his eyes toward others' worldly enjoyment because the provision of his Lord is better and more lasting; desire is redirected to its true source.
If God expanded provision without measure people would transgress, so He sends it down in the amount He wills; the wide vessel and large gift require a governing limit.
Appetites for family, wealth, livestock, and cultivation are made alluring, but the ayah calls them only the provision of the nearer life.
The answer to worldly appetites in 3:14 is a better gift with their Lord, redirecting desire from transient contents toward its lasting destination.

تَرْغَبُونَ أَن تَنكِحُوهُنَّ uses the رغبة root around orphan women and justice; because the construction permits desire to marry or aversion from marrying, it only tentatively shows appetite being disciplined by another's rights.
